A: The headphones I ordered last week arrived yesterday, but the left side doesn't work.
B: I'm sorry to hear that. We can exchange them or give you a refund.
A: I'd like to exchange them, please.
B: Please send them back with the form in the box. Shipping is free.
A: How long will it take to get the new ones?

Here is the plan for Volunteer Day. Group A, meet me at the school gate, because you will put new flowers in the beds along the front path. Group B, take the bus to the nursery school; you will be reading picture books to the children there. Group C goes to Riverside Park to collect rubbish along the water. And Group D, at the station square, will give the old wall by the bike park a fresh coat of paint. Bring gloves, everyone. We had planned to wash the library windows too, but that job has been put off until next term.

話者1: A haunted house would be really exciting. We'd have to buy black curtains and costumes, though, so it isn't cheap. And we'd need about fifteen people to scare the visitors properly. The good news is that each tour only takes ten minutes.
話者2: How about a magic show? The cards and ropes are already in our classroom, so we don't have to spend a single yen. Two of us perform and three guide the audience — five people in total. Each show runs for twenty minutes.
話者3: A café sounds nice. We could bring tea bags from home, but we'd still have to buy cups, sugar and cookies. Eight of us could run it easily, and customers usually stay for about twenty minutes.
話者4: Let's do a giant puzzle corner. The art club will lend us their puzzle for free, and only three of us are needed at a time. The one problem is the time — finishing one puzzle takes about forty-five minutes.

Good afternoon. Tonight, while you sleep, your brain will be busy sorting through everything that happened today. Let me explain what we now know about sleep and memory.

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as a kind of switching off. Textbooks described the sleeping brain as idle, simply waiting for morning. Students were told that if they wanted to remember something, the answer was more hours of study, and sleep was time taken away from that study.

The picture changed in the nineteen nineties, when researchers began recording brain activity through the night. They found that the patterns produced while an animal learned a maze during the day were played again during sleep, faster and in the same order. Nothing was switching off at all.

We now think of sleep as the stage where a memory becomes permanent. During the day, new information is held in a small structure near the centre of the brain. At night, the same information is copied out to the outer surface, where it can last for years. Wake someone repeatedly during the deepest stage of sleep, and the copying never finishes.

There is a second effect, and it is easier to demonstrate. Give two groups a list of word pairs. Let one group sleep for eight hours and keep the other awake for the same eight hours. Test them the next evening, when both are equally tired. The group that slept remembers about forty per cent more. So sleep is not a gap in learning. It is part of the process, and it cannot be replaced by extra hours at the desk.

Suki: Ethan, we have to submit our presentation format by Thursday and I keep changing my mind. Remind me what the four are.
Ethan: The lecture format is twenty minutes on stage in the big hall. The poster format puts you beside a printed board while people walk up and ask things. The filmed format means you record everything in advance and the panel watches it later. And the seminar format is a small room, ten people, and a discussion afterwards.
Suki: I assumed I'd take the lecture format. My whole year will be in that hall, and I want them to actually hear what I found.
Ethan: That's fair, but the poster format has something the stage can't give you. Strangers come up and ask the question you never thought of, and you have to answer it right there. I left mine last year with three ideas I'd never have had alone.
Suki: Questions I haven't prepared for. That's exactly what I'm most afraid of and probably what I need.
Ethan: And nobody is watching a clock, so a good conversation can run for half an hour.
Suki: All right, I'm not giving up that back-and-forth. I'll pick a format that has it.
Ethan: So you'll be standing next to a poster with me on Friday?
Suki: No, I still want a proper audience sitting down and listening to the whole argument from start to finish.

Fintan: Doctor Hale stopped mid-sentence today and simply looked at the back row. Four phones face up on the desks, and every one of them lit up while she stood there waiting.
Marisol: Mine was one of the four and I will not pretend otherwise. It stays on the desk because I want to know at once if somebody needs me.
Gwen: The department ran a survey about exactly this last term. Of all the students who admitted checking their phone in class, two hundred and sixty said they did it because a notification had appeared on the screen, which was more than any other reason.
Fintan: So it is not that people want to look. The screen asks them to, and they answer it.
Gwen: Boredom came second, at about a hundred and seventy five. Family messages were much lower, and hardly anybody said they were checking the time.
Marisol: Two hundred and sixty out of how many, though? That number means nothing on its own.
Gwen: Out of six hundred who answered. So nearly half the year group loses the thread of a lecture because a screen flashed at them.
Fintan: That is me, then. I will put mine in my bag from Monday rather than let a notification decide when I stop listening.
Marisol: You are both looking at me now, and I can feel it.
Gwen: I am in no position to look at anybody. Mine has been face down beside my pen for this entire conversation, so I will start doing the thing I am telling everyone else to do.
Marisol: Fine. Not because either of you asked me, but because I do not like being one of two hundred and sixty. It goes in the bag.
Fintan: Witnessed, and I am telling Doctor Hale on Monday.
It's too hot in here. Do you mind if I turn on the air conditioner?

W: Do you have this shirt in a smaller size?
M: We have small and extra-small. Which would you like?
W: Small, please. And in blue if possible.
M: Sure, here's a small blue one.

A: Can I borrow this book for three weeks?
B: Usually two weeks is the limit, but new books are just one week.

Now, about our four areas. The Reading Room closes at eight, and you may bring a drink, but only in a bottle with a lid — no open cups. The Study Booths stay open the longest, right up to nine, though you do need to book one first. The Group Room shuts at six and, as the name suggests, it cannot be used by fewer than four people. And the Café Corner, where drinks are of course fine, closes two hours before the Reading Room does.

Good morning. Today we look at vertical farming: growing food in stacked layers inside buildings, under electric light, in the middle of a city. It sounds futuristic, but the first commercial farms of this kind opened only about fifteen years ago.

Start with a simple question: where does a city's salad come from? In most cities, lettuce is trucked in from farms hundreds of kilometres away. That journey costs money and the leaves lose freshness before they reach the shelf. Farming closer to the city sounds obvious, but around most large cities there is very little land left.

Vertical farms answer this by moving indoors. Because the building controls temperature and light, the season outside stops mattering, and you can harvest lettuce in January in a cold climate. Many of these farms occupy abandoned warehouses, which are cheap and already wired for electricity.

The water story surprises people. In an open field, most of the water you apply sinks into the soil or evaporates. In a closed indoor system, the same water goes around the system again and again, so one of these farms can use ninety per cent less water than a field growing the identical crop.

Space works differently too. A field can only get bigger sideways. Indoors, when you want more growing area, you stack another layer on top rather than buy another field, so ten layers in one building equal ten fields of surface. The difficulty is electricity. Lighting is the single largest cost, and researchers are still testing which crops earn that cost back. Leafy greens do. Wheat, so far, does not.

Marco: Priya, the meal plan form is due Friday and I've read it four times without understanding it. What are the actual choices?
Priya: Four of them. The full plan gives you three meals a day in the dining hall. The dinner plan is just the evening meal there. The credit plan loads money onto your card and you spend it anywhere on campus. And the weekday plan feeds you Monday to Friday, with weekends left to you.
Marco: The full plan sounds safest. I'd never have to think about food again, and I'd see people at every meal instead of eating alone in my room.
Priya: It's safe, but think about what the credit plan lets you do. Whatever money you don't spend rolls over to the next term instead of vanishing, and I saved enough last year to cover a whole week in Lisbon.
Marco: Money that doesn't disappear at the end of term. That is worth something.
Priya: And you can use it at the late-night cafe, which the dining hall plans don't cover at all.
Marco: Okay, I don't want to lose that rollover. I'll choose a plan that keeps it.
Priya: So you'll be on the credit plan with me?
Marco: No, I still want someone to hand me a hot dinner at the end of a long day.

Colin: The school sent another notice about helmets today. Third one this term. I've cycled here for three years without one and nothing has ever happened, so I don't really see the point of all this paperwork.
Riko: Same here. And they flatten my hair for the entire morning, no matter what I do to it beforehand. I'm not walking into class looking like that.
Bianca: I put mine on every single day, so the notice wasn't really aimed at me.
Colin: Wait, seriously? You've never once ridden without it, not even down to the shops?
Bianca: Not since I started. It seems like a small thing until you look at what happens here. Last year in this city, forty-two students were taken to hospital with head injuries after bicycle crashes.
Riko: Forty-two out of how many people, though? That could be a tiny share of everyone who rides.
Bianca: I looked it up because I wanted the same answer. Of every student the hospital treated after a crash, head injuries were the largest group of all. Broken arms came second, at about twenty-five.
Colin: Head injuries beating everything else, including arms and legs. That's actually the part that gets me.
Riko: It gets me too, but I still think the road near school is slow enough. If I had to wear that thing every morning, I'd rather just walk.
Colin: I think I'll start keeping one on the bike from tomorrow rather than argue with the school about it.
Bianca: You'll forget it once, feel the wind on your head, and then never forget it again.
Riko: Fine, but don't expect me in one.
I usually play tennis on Sundays, but this week I have a part-time job.

W: They're on the second floor. The dolphins are on the first floor.
M: Then let's start with dolphins and then go up to penguins.
W: OK, but let's skip the shark tank. We saw it last time.

B: Usually two weeks is the limit, but new books are just one week.
A: This one was published last month.
B: Then it's one week. But you can renew it once online.
A: OK, I'll do that if I need more time.

Last Saturday I went to the open day at Midtown High, and I'd like to tell you what I did. First, all the visitors gathered in the gym for a welcome talk by the principal. After that, I went straight to the music room and got to try a violin for the very first time. Then I spent about half an hour in the library, reading their collection of old newspapers. To finish the day, I had a piece of chocolate cake in the cafeteria. I did want to see the chemistry experiment, but the science room was closed for repairs.

Nadia: Owen, registration closes tonight and I still can't decide on the Spanish course. There are four formats, aren't there?
Owen: Four. The evening class meets on campus twice a week. The recorded course gives you video lessons you watch whenever you like. The streamed course meets online at a fixed hour. And the mixed course puts you in the classroom every other week and online the rest of the time.
Nadia: I was leaning towards the evening class. I want to speak out loud, and honestly I want to meet people. Sitting alone with a laptop for a whole term sounds miserable.
Owen: I understand that, but look at what the recorded course adds. Every unit comes with a speaking bot you can argue with as long as you want, and it never gets tired of you. I found it genuinely amusing, and my accent improved more in a month than it did all last year.
Nadia: A bot that doesn't sigh at my grammar. That is tempting.
Owen: And the written feedback comes back the same evening instead of the following week.
Nadia: Right, I don't want to give up those extras. I'll sign up for something that includes them.
Owen: So you're joining me in the recorded course after all?
Nadia: No, I still want to walk into a real classroom sometimes and hear other students trying.

Jonah: Coach moved morning practice to seven again. I only just make the old time, and that was with running the last two blocks.
Meera: I catch the seven-ten bus, so seven o'clock practice is mathematically impossible for me. Something has to change.
Silas: I leave home at six twenty every morning anyway, so the new time makes no difference to me at all.
Jonah: Six twenty? Even on the mornings when there's no practice at all?
Silas: Every morning, all year. And it's worth it, because I checked the club book last week. Of everyone who missed the qualifying round over the last three years, eighty-one people missed it because of late arrival at practice, which was more than any other reason.
Meera: Eighty-one? More than injuries? I assumed injuries would be top by a long way.
Silas: Injuries came second, at about fifty-four. Late arrival was well clear of it, and illness was lower still.
Jonah: So the thing most likely to keep me out of the qualifier is my own alarm clock. That is a genuinely depressing sentence.
Meera: It changes things for me too. I'll take the six forty bus from tomorrow instead of arguing about the schedule.
Jonah: Then I'm setting my alarm twenty minutes earlier, starting tonight. I'd rather lose the sleep than the round.
Silas: You'll both hate me for two weeks and then stop noticing it.
Meera: We already hate you. Nobody should be that awake before seven in the morning.
The concert starts at seven, but let's meet at the station at six to get good seats.

M: It's going to rain on Saturday, our first day.
W: And Sunday?
M: Cloudy, but no rain.
W: Good, we can go hiking on Sunday, then.

A: The pandas are the most popular. The line is already long.
B: Can we see them last, then?
A: Good idea. We'll start with the elephants near the entrance.
B: And the monkeys after that?
A: Sure. Then lunch, and the pandas in the afternoon when the line is shorter.

Good morning, everyone. Today I'll show you how I make my favorite pancakes. To start off, put the flour, eggs and milk in a bowl and mix them until smooth. Next, pour the batter into a hot frying pan and cook one side until small bubbles appear on the surface. When you see those bubbles, flip it over and cook the other side for about a minute. Finally, slide it onto a plate and pour plenty of maple syrup on top. And by the way, you never need an oven for this recipe.

Otto: They're extending the library to eleven at night from next month. I thought the two of you would be pleased about that.
Naoki: Not especially. I've been working in the cafe on the corner all year because the library closed before I even got started.
Freya: The cafe is nice, though. Nobody glares at you for opening a packet of crisps in there.
Otto: Fair, but the university asked people why they stopped using the library, and the answer wasn't crisps. Of everyone who said they'd given up on it, a hundred and sixty people named the closing time, which was ahead of every other reason.
Naoki: A hundred and sixty for the closing time? I would have guessed noise, honestly.
Otto: Noise came second, at about ninety. Closing time was well clear of it, and lack of desks was lower again.
Freya: That's a strong argument, actually. If the hours were the real problem, then fixing the hours fixes most of it.
Naoki: I suppose I can't complain about the closing time and then ignore it when they change it.
Otto: That does sound like the trap you've walked into, yes.
Naoki: Fine. I'll move back in there from next month rather than pay four pounds a night for a coffee I don't drink.
Freya: Good for you. I'll keep cheering from the cafe, obviously. My table by the window has my name on it now.
Otto: So you agree with all of it and change nothing. That's very consistent of you.
The bus was late again, so I missed the first ten minutes of the movie.

話者2: The badminton class meets in the school gym, and rackets and shuttles are all provided by us. We take complete beginners every term, and about half the members this year had never played before joining.
話者3: The running class is perfect for beginners, and you need nothing but the shoes you already own. Of course we run along the river and through the park, so we are outside in all weather, even in winter.
話者4: The climbing class takes place on an indoor wall, and anyone can join from their very first day. One thing to know is that each member has to buy their own shoes and harness, which comes to about nine thousand yen.

Elodie: Tariq, I have to book the venue for the practice match today. Talk me through the four again, slowly.
Tariq: The school gym is free but the ceiling is low. The city arena is proper height and has seating, but it costs eighty pounds an hour. The park courts are outdoors and free, and completely at the mercy of the weather. And the community centre is indoors, half the arena price, with a small balcony for spectators.
Elodie: I'd assumed the school gym. It's free, it's five minutes from the classrooms, and nobody has to travel anywhere.
Tariq: Except the ceiling. Every high serve we practise in there dies against the roof, so we arrive at real matches having never played a proper lift. The arena fixed that for us in one afternoon last year.
Elodie: So the gym is quietly teaching us the wrong game. I hadn't thought about it like that.
Tariq: And a real ceiling means the visiting team takes us seriously from the first point.
Elodie: Fine, I won't book anywhere with a low roof. It has to be full height.
Tariq: So I can tell the arena we're coming on Saturday?
Elodie: No, we still cannot spend eighty pounds an hour out of a budget that has forty left in it.

Piers: The canteen has put up another sign about returning trays. That's the third one this term, which rather suggests the first two didn't work.
Callum: I leave mine, I'll admit it freely. There's always someone clearing tables anyway, so it never really felt like it mattered much.
Yuna: I'd return mine happily if the racks weren't right beside the entrance. Walking back against everyone coming in is genuinely unpleasant at half past twelve.
Piers: They counted it properly this month, though, and the numbers are worse than I expected. Of all the trays left behind in one week, four hundred and thirty were abandoned during the lunch hour, which was more than any other time of day.
Callum: Four hundred and thirty in a single week? At lunchtime alone?
Piers: Breakfast came second, at about a hundred and ninety. Lunch was well ahead of it, and the evening was lower still.
Yuna: That is a lot of trays. Fine, I'll do it the day they move the racks to the far wall.
Piers: They said last year that they have no plans to move them at all. The plumbing runs behind that wall.
Yuna: Then my offer stands exactly as it is.
Callum: I can't defend mine any more, honestly. I'll carry my own tray over from tomorrow instead of waiting for someone else to do it.
Piers: I've taken mine back since first year, so I'll just keep quietly doing that.
Callum: You've been unbearably right for this entire conversation, you know.
The train was crowded this morning, so I had to stand all the way to the office.

M: I'll drive from the house. You're coming on foot, right?
W: Yes. Shall we meet by the lake on the way?
M: The road there is a dead end for cars. Let me pick you up after the bridge.
W: All right, right where the road turns into the campsite.

A: We're out of milk and eggs.
B: I'll stop by the supermarket on my way home.
A: Can you also get bread? Not the white one ̶ the whole grain one.
B: Sure. Anything else?
A: No, that's all. Oh wait ̶ do we have butter?
B: Yes, I bought some yesterday.

Rafferty: Nadine, the group booking closes at midnight and I still haven't picked how we're getting there. Run the four past me.
Nadine: The night bus is the cheapest by far and takes eleven hours. The flight is ninety minutes but you lose most of the saving to the airport transfers. The express train is four hours, twice the bus price, with a proper table to sit at. And the rental van is one price split between us, and one of us has to drive the whole way.
Rafferty: I'd been assuming the night bus. It's the cheapest thing on the list and we're all broke after this term.
Nadine: It's cheap, but count what it actually costs you. Eleven hours upright means you arrive unable to think, and we lose the first day of a four-day trip to everyone sleeping it off. The train got us there before lunch last year.
Rafferty: So the cheap option quietly eats a quarter of the holiday. That's a real number, put like that.
Nadine: And on the train we can actually sit facing each other and plan the days properly.

Good morning. Today we look at vertical farming: growing food in stacked layers inside buildings, under electric light, in the middle of a city. It sounds futuristic, but the first commercial farms of this kind opened only about fifteen years ago.

Start with a simple question: where does a city's salad come from? In most cities, lettuce is trucked in from farms hundreds of kilometres away. That journey costs money and the leaves lose freshness before they reach the shelf. Farming closer to the city sounds obvious, but around most large cities there is very little land left.

Vertical farms answer this by moving indoors. Because the building controls temperature and light, the season outside stops mattering, and you can harvest lettuce in January in a cold climate. Many of these farms occupy abandoned warehouses, which are cheap and already wired for electricity.

The water story surprises people. In an open field, most of the water you apply sinks into the soil or evaporates. In a closed indoor system, the same water goes around the system again and again, so one of these farms can use ninety per cent less water than a field growing the identical crop.

Space works differently too. A field can only get bigger sideways. Indoors, when you want more growing area, you stack another layer on top rather than buy another field, so ten layers in one building equal ten fields of surface. The difficulty is electricity. Lighting is the single largest cost, and researchers are still testing which crops earn that cost back. Leafy greens do. Wheat, so far, does not.

Good morning. Electric cars are often discussed as a battery problem. I want to argue that the harder problem is where the electricity is delivered.

Start with the battery. In two thousand ten, a battery pack cost around one thousand one hundred dollars per kilowatt hour. Today it is under a hundred and forty. That is one of the fastest cost reductions in industrial history, and an electric car and a petrol car now cost roughly the same to build.

So why has adoption been so patchy? Survey after survey gives the same answer, and it is not price. Buyers say they are afraid of running out of charge on a long journey. Notice, though, that this fear does not match how people actually drive. The average daily distance in most countries is under fifty kilometres, well within any modern car's range. What buyers are really telling us is that they do not trust the network of charging points, not that they need a bigger battery.

And the numbers support them. Where those chargers sit is another matter. In several European countries there is one charger for every ten electric cars; in others the figure is one for every forty. Worse, roughly one in five public chargers is out of order at any moment, and a driver cannot know before arriving.

Which points to the real lesson. Home charging solves this for anyone with a driveway, and about eighty per cent of charging already happens overnight at home. But in cities, most people park on the street, and for them no driveway means no overnight charging. So the group least able to charge conveniently is the urban population, exactly the group cities most want to move out of petrol cars.

Good afternoon. Tonight, while you sleep, your brain will be busy sorting through everything that happened today. Let me explain what we now know about sleep and memory.

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as a kind of switching off. Textbooks described the sleeping brain as idle, simply waiting for morning. Students were told that if they wanted to remember something, the answer was more hours of study, and sleep was time taken away from that study.

The picture changed in the nineteen nineties, when researchers began recording brain activity through the night. They found that the patterns produced while an animal learned a maze during the day were played again during sleep, faster and in the same order. Nothing was switching off at all.

We now think of sleep as the stage where a memory becomes permanent. During the day, new information is held in a small structure near the centre of the brain. At night, the same information is copied out to the outer surface, where it can last for years. Wake someone repeatedly during the deepest stage of sleep, and the copying never finishes.

There is a second effect, and it is easier to demonstrate. Give two groups a list of word pairs. Let one group sleep for eight hours and keep the other awake for the same eight hours. Test them the next evening, when both are equally tired. The group that slept remembers about forty per cent more. So sleep is not a gap in learning. It is part of the process, and it cannot be replaced by extra hours at the desk.

Good morning. Today's topic is the bicycle sharing system, and I want to use it to show you how a small design decision can decide whether a public service works.

The first generation appeared in Amsterdam in nineteen sixty-five. White bicycles were left unlocked around the city for anyone to use. The idea was beautiful and it collapsed within a month, because almost every bicycle was stolen or thrown into a canal. For thirty years afterwards, city governments treated the whole concept as impossible.

The second generation added coin locks, but it did not fix the deeper problem. Nobody knew who had taken a bicycle, so nobody was answerable for it. What changed everything in the two thousands was not the bicycle. It was the card reader. Once each trip is linked to a named account, the bicycle stops being anonymous, and losses fall to a level a city can live with.

That brings us to today's numbers. In the largest systems, each bicycle is now used between four and eight times a day. Compare that with a privately owned bicycle, which sits unused for more than twenty-three hours out of twenty-four. The same piece of metal serves many more people.

And yet these systems rarely pay for themselves. Riders' fees typically cover about fifty per cent of the running cost. The heaviest expense is not repair. It is trucks, moving bicycles back uphill and out of the centre every night, because riders take them downhill in the morning and leave them there. Some cities now pay riders a small credit for returning a bicycle to an empty station, which is cheaper than sending a truck.

Good morning. There are about seven thousand languages spoken today, and by the end of this century linguists expect roughly half of them to have no speakers left. I want to look at how that happens, and at what the standard response gets wrong.

First, how a language ends. It is almost never sudden. The usual pattern takes three generations. Grandparents speak the local language at home. Parents understand it but answer their own children in the national language, because that is the language of school and work. The grandchildren can follow a conversation but cannot produce a sentence. Nothing is banned and nobody decides. Each family simply makes a reasonable choice, and the sum of those choices ends a language.

Second, what linguists do about it. For most of the twentieth century, the response was documentation. Send a researcher, record the last fluent speakers, write a grammar and a dictionary, and place them in a university archive. The tapes are safe. Nobody listens to them.

And this is where I want to be blunt. A recorded language is not a living one. A grammar in an archive lets a scholar study a language; it does not let a child grow up in it. If the goal is speakers rather than data, the work has to happen where families make daily decisions.

There is one encouraging case. Hebrew had no native speakers for centuries and now has millions. But look at what it required: a state, a school system, and an army all operating in the language. No archive did that. Which means archives are worth keeping, but nobody should mistake them for a rescue.

Good afternoon. Tonight, while you sleep, your brain will be busy sorting through everything that happened today. Let me explain what we now know about sleep and memory.

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as a kind of switching off. Textbooks described the sleeping brain as idle, simply waiting for morning. Students were told that if they wanted to remember something, the answer was more hours of study, and sleep was time taken away from that study.

The picture changed in the nineteen nineties, when researchers began recording brain activity through the night. They found that the patterns produced while an animal learned a maze during the day were played again during sleep, faster and in the same order. Nothing was switching off at all.

We now think of sleep as the stage where a memory becomes permanent. During the day, new information is held in a small structure near the centre of the brain. At night, the same information is copied out to the outer surface, where it can last for years. Wake someone repeatedly during the deepest stage of sleep, and the copying never finishes.

There is a second effect, and it is easier to demonstrate. Give two groups a list of word pairs. Let one group sleep for eight hours and keep the other awake for the same eight hours. Test them the next evening, when both are equally tired. The group that slept remembers about forty per cent more. So sleep is not a gap in learning. It is part of the process, and it cannot be replaced by extra hours at the desk.

Good morning. About one bite in three of the food on your plate exists because an insect visited a flower. Today I want to look at who those insects actually are.

When people talk about pollination, they usually mean one species: the honeybee. Honeybees are easy to keep, easy to move, and a single hive holds tens of thousands of workers. So for decades, growers of almonds, apples and blueberries have solved pollination by renting hives, trucking them in when the flowers open and taking them away afterwards.

That approach has been under pressure since two thousand six, when beekeepers in North America began losing around a third of their hives each winter. The causes are still argued about, but the effect on growers is simple. The price of renting a hive has roughly tripled in twenty years.

Here is the part that surprises people. Honeybees are not always the best pollinators. A honeybee packs pollen tightly onto its legs to carry it home, which means less of it rubs off on the next flower. A bumblebee is messier, and messier is better. Bumblebees also work in cool, wet weather that keeps honeybees inside the hive.

And wild insects are already doing far more than growers assume. Careful counts in orchards show that wild bees and flies, arriving with no rent to pay, carry out roughly half the pollination even in fields where hives have been placed. Those insects need hedges and rough ground near the orchard. A farm that removes every hedge to gain a little planting area is quietly paying for something it used to get free.

There is a second effect, and it is easier to demonstrate. Give two groups a list of word pairs. Let one group sleep for eight hours and keep the other awake for the same eight hours. Test them the next evening, when both are equally tired. The group that slept remembers about forty per cent more. So sleep is not a gap in learning. It is part of the process, and it cannot be replaced by extra hours at the desk.

Good morning. You paid something like four dollars for a cup of coffee this morning. Today I want to follow that four dollars backwards, from your hand to the farm, because the shape of the answer tells you a lot about international trade.

Of your four dollars, the farmer who grew the beans receives somewhere between three and ten cents. The rest is divided among shipping, roasting, packaging, the shop's rent, and the wages of the person who served you. This is not a story of one greedy company. It is the ordinary arithmetic of a long chain.

Why so little at the farm end? Because the farmer sells the cheapest version of the product. Green coffee, unroasted, is a commodity. Any sack is interchangeable with any other sack of the same grade, so the price is set on a world exchange and no individual grower can influence it. Meanwhile, the roasted, branded, ground coffee in your cup is not interchangeable at all, and whoever owns that stage sets their own price.

So the interesting question is where along the chain value gets added. And notice what that implies. If a producing country roasts and packages its own coffee, it captures far more of the final price. Ethiopia has been trying exactly this for two decades.

But it is harder than it sounds. Roasted coffee goes stale within weeks, so shipping it means air freight or refrigeration. Importing countries also charge a far heavier duty on roasted coffee than on green beans, which quietly discourages the very step that would help. And building recognised brands abroad takes money that a small grower simply does not have.

Good morning. Today's story is about the simplest medical intervention ever discovered, and about how long it took to be accepted.

Vienna, eighteen forty-seven. A young doctor named Semmelweis worked in a hospital with two maternity wards. In the first ward, staffed by doctors, about one mother in ten died after giving birth. In the second, staffed by midwives, the figure was closer to one in thirty. The wards took women on alternate days, so the patients were not different. Something about the first ward was killing them.

Semmelweis noticed that the doctors, unlike the midwives, came straight from performing autopsies. He could not explain why that mattered, because nobody yet knew that microbes existed. But he insisted that every doctor rinse his hands in a chlorine solution before entering the ward. Deaths in the first ward fell to the level of the second within a year.

And here is the uncomfortable part. His colleagues rejected him. Some were insulted by the suggestion that a gentleman's hands could be dirty. Others pointed out, correctly, that he had no theory to explain the result. Semmelweis was eventually dismissed from the hospital, and hand washing was not general practice for another forty years, until Pasteur's work made the mechanism clear.

The modern lesson is not just historical. Studies in today's hospitals find that staff clean their hands on well under half the occasions when guidelines require it. And the reason given is almost never disagreement. It is time. A nurse on a busy ward may have dozens of such occasions in an hour, and the sink is not always close by. So the barrier has moved from belief to design.

Hanae: Marcus, I have to answer by Friday and I still cannot choose. Go through the four with me again.
Marcus: The cafe pays eight fifty an hour, shifts finish at ten, and you choose your days. The bookshop pays about the same, but it is whole weekends, Saturday and Sunday, nothing midweek. The tutoring centre pays fourteen, teaching maths to fifteen year olds. And the delivery job pays the most of any of them, because the shifts run from nine until one in the morning.
Hanae: Fourteen an hour is nearly double the cafe. I had been leaning towards the tutoring centre just for that.
Marcus: Look at what the money costs you. My brother took the delivery job last year for exactly that reason, and the money is meaningless if you sleep through the lecture you are paying for. He failed two modules and repeated the year.
Hanae: So a high hourly rate can quietly take away the thing I came here to do.
Marcus: Exactly. Wages you can earn again later. A repeated year you cannot.
Hanae: Right. I will not take anything that has me finishing after midnight. That settles at least one of them.
Marcus: So shall I tell the tutoring centre you are interested? It is the best paid of the three left.
Hanae: No, and I cannot teach maths to anyone, so that is out as well. And you know I have practice both days at the weekend.

Hello everyone. When you picture plastic in the ocean, you probably picture a beach. Today I want to move your attention upstream, to rivers.

For twenty years, ocean clean-up campaigns focused almost entirely on the shoreline. Volunteers walked beaches with bags, and the photographs were powerful. But once plastic reaches open water, it breaks into pieces smaller than a grain of rice, and at that size no net can pick it up. Removing it out there costs roughly a hundred times what it costs to stop it on land.

That is why attention has shifted to rivers. A recent survey traced the plastic entering the sea and found something unexpected: a very small number of rivers carry the great majority of it. Just over a thousand rivers, out of about a hundred thousand worldwide, account for eighty per cent of the plastic reaching the ocean. Almost all of these are short rivers running through dense cities where waste collection has not kept pace with population growth.

This changes what a solution looks like. Instead of one global campaign, you can place barriers at a small number of specific points, because a floating barrier across a river mouth catches material while it is still large enough to grab.

But I want to be careful here. Barriers treat the symptom. The plastic still has to be paid for by someone, and in many of these cities the real gap is that rubbish is never picked up in the first place. A barrier is also useless during floods, when it must be opened. So the honest summary is this: rivers give us a cheaper place to act, not a complete answer.

Good morning. Today's topic is the bicycle sharing system, and I want to use it to show you how a small design decision can decide whether a public service works.

The first generation appeared in Amsterdam in nineteen sixty-five. White bicycles were left unlocked around the city for anyone to use. The idea was beautiful and it collapsed within a month, because almost every bicycle was stolen or thrown into a canal. For thirty years afterwards, city governments treated the whole concept as impossible.

The second generation added coin locks, but it did not fix the deeper problem. Nobody knew who had taken a bicycle, so nobody was answerable for it. What changed everything in the two thousands was not the bicycle. It was the card reader. Once each trip is linked to a named account, the bicycle stops being anonymous, and losses fall to a level a city can live with.

That brings us to today's numbers. In the largest systems, each bicycle is now used between four and eight times a day. Compare that with a privately owned bicycle, which sits unused for more than twenty-three hours out of twenty-four. The same piece of metal serves many more people.

And yet these systems rarely pay for themselves. Riders' fees typically cover about fifty per cent of the running cost. The heaviest expense is not repair. It is trucks, moving bicycles back uphill and out of the centre every night, because riders take them downhill in the morning and leave them there. Some cities now pay riders a small credit for returning a bicycle to an empty station, which is cheaper than sending a truck.

Good morning. Today we look at vertical farming: growing food in stacked layers inside buildings, under electric light, in the middle of a city. It sounds futuristic, but the first commercial farms of this kind opened only about fifteen years ago.

Start with a simple question: where does a city's salad come from? In most cities, lettuce is trucked in from farms hundreds of kilometres away. That journey costs money and the leaves lose freshness before they reach the shelf. Farming closer to the city sounds obvious, but around most large cities there is very little land left.

Vertical farms answer this by moving indoors. Because the building controls temperature and light, the season outside stops mattering, and you can harvest lettuce in January in a cold climate. Many of these farms occupy abandoned warehouses, which are cheap and already wired for electricity.

The water story surprises people. In an open field, most of the water you apply sinks into the soil or evaporates. In a closed indoor system, the same water goes around the system again and again, so one of these farms can use ninety per cent less water than a field growing the identical crop.

Space works differently too. A field can only get bigger sideways. Indoors, when you want more growing area, you stack another layer on top rather than buy another field, so ten layers in one building equal ten fields of surface. The difficulty is electricity. Lighting is the single largest cost, and researchers are still testing which crops earn that cost back. Leafy greens do. Wheat, so far, does not.

People often ask how we put a broken pot back together. Nothing can begin until every piece is spread out on the table so that we can see the whole puzzle. 話者2: Small birds are cheap; a pair and a cage together come to around two thousand yen. They also need fresh water and food every single morning, weekend or not. And I should warn you that they sing very loudly at sunrise.

Good morning. There are about seven thousand languages spoken today, and by the end of this century linguists expect roughly half of them to have no speakers left. I want to look at how that happens, and at what the standard response gets wrong.

First, how a language ends. It is almost never sudden. The usual pattern takes three generations. Grandparents speak the local language at home. Parents understand it but answer their own children in the national language, because that is the language of school and work. The grandchildren can follow a conversation but cannot produce a sentence. Nothing is banned and nobody decides. Each family simply makes a reasonable choice, and the sum of those choices ends a language.

Second, what linguists do about it. For most of the twentieth century, the response was documentation. Send a researcher, record the last fluent speakers, write a grammar and a dictionary, and place them in a university archive. The tapes are safe. Nobody listens to them.

And this is where I want to be blunt. A recorded language is not a living one. A grammar in an archive lets a scholar study a language; it does not let a child grow up in it. If the goal is speakers rather than data, the work has to happen where families make daily decisions.

There is one encouraging case. Hebrew had no native speakers for centuries and now has millions. But look at what it required: a state, a school system, and an army all operating in the language. No archive did that. Which means archives are worth keeping, but nobody should mistake them for a rescue.

Good afternoon. Roughly a third of the food grown in the world is never eaten. Today I want to be precise about where in the chain that food is lost, because the answer decides what you should do about it.

There is a common assumption that waste is mainly a consumer failure: shoppers buying too much and throwing it away. Public campaigns have followed this assumption for years, with posters about planning your meals and checking your fridge.

But the picture depends entirely on which country you look at. In low income countries, most of the loss happens before the food ever reaches a shop. Grain sits in the open and gets wet before anyone can store it. Vegetables travel for days in unrefrigerated trucks on poor roads, and much of a harvest can be gone by the time it arrives. There, food never reaches consumers at all, so consumer advice is beside the point.

In high income countries the pattern inverts. Storage and transport are good, and the largest single share is lost in kitchens, both household and restaurant. So the same global figure hides two completely different problems requiring two different remedies.

One further point, and it is the one people find least intuitive. Not all waste weighs the same environmentally. A kilogram of beef thrown away represents around sixty times the greenhouse emissions of a kilogram of potatoes, because of everything that went into producing it. So a campaign that reduces the total weight of waste may achieve very little, while a campaign focused narrowly on meat and dairy could achieve a great deal. Weight is the easy thing to measure. It is not the thing that matters.

Elodie: Tariq, I have to book the venue for the practice match today. Talk me through the four again, slowly.

Elodie: I'd assumed the school gym. It's free, it's five minutes from the classrooms, and nobody has to travel anywhere.

Good morning. About one bite in three of the food on your plate exists because an insect visited a flower. Today I want to look at who those insects actually are.

When people talk about pollination, they usually mean one species: the honeybee. Honeybees are easy to keep, easy to move, and a single hive holds tens of thousands of workers. So for decades, growers of almonds, apples and blueberries have solved pollination by renting hives, trucking them in when the flowers open and taking them away afterwards.

That approach has been under pressure since two thousand six, when beekeepers in North America began losing around a third of their hives each winter. The causes are still argued about, but the effect on growers is simple. The price of renting a hive has roughly tripled in twenty years.

Here is the part that surprises people. Honeybees are not always the best pollinators. A honeybee packs pollen tightly onto its legs to carry it home, which means less of it rubs off on the next flower. A bumblebee is messier, and messier is better. Bumblebees also work in cool, wet weather that keeps honeybees inside the hive.

And wild insects are already doing far more than growers assume. Careful counts in orchards show that wild bees and flies, arriving with no rent to pay, carry out roughly half the pollination even in fields where hives have been placed. Those insects need hedges and rough ground near the orchard. A farm that removes every hedge to gain a little planting area is quietly paying for something it used to get free.

Kwame: Rosalind, housing applications open Monday and I have four boxes to choose between. What did they actually mean by all of them?
Rosalind: The hall gives you a single room on campus with a canteen downstairs. The homestay puts you with a local family and they cook for you. The shared flat is four students, one kitchen, and rent split four ways. And the studio is your own tiny place off campus with nobody else in it.
Kwame: I had the studio circled. I write at strange hours and I hate explaining myself to anyone about it.
Rosalind: I understand, but the shared flat gave me something a studio never could. Rent split four ways came to less than half what the studio costs, and I ate properly because somebody was always cooking something.
Kwame: Less than half. That's a whole extra term of savings, put like that.
Rosalind: And when I got ill in February, three people noticed within a day.
Kwame: Right, I don't want to lose that cheaper rent. I'll apply for something that keeps it.
Rosalind: So you're taking a room in a shared flat like I did?
Kwame: No, I still want someone older around who notices when I've stopped eating properly.

Zane: I nearly took out a first-year outside the staff room this morning. He came round the corner just as I did, and neither of us was going slowly.

examples.script:
Good morning. Electric cars are often discussed as a battery problem. I want to argue that the harder problem is where the electricity is delivered.

Start with the battery. In two thousand ten, a battery pack cost around one thousand one hundred dollars per kilowatt hour. Today it is under a hundred and forty. That is one of the fastest cost reductions in industrial history, and an electric car and a petrol car now cost roughly the same to build.

So why has adoption been so patchy? Survey after survey gives the same answer, and it is not price. Buyers say they are afraid of running out of charge on a long journey. Notice, though, that this fear does not match how people actually drive. The average daily distance in most countries is under fifty kilometres, well within any modern car's range. What buyers are really telling us is that they do not trust the network of charging points, not that they need a bigger battery.

And the numbers support them. Where those chargers sit is another matter. In several European countries there is one charger for every ten electric cars; in others the figure is one for every forty. Worse, roughly one in five public chargers is out of order at any moment, and a driver cannot know before arriving.

Which points to the real lesson. Home charging solves this for anyone with a driveway, and about eighty per cent of charging already happens overnight at home. But in cities, most people park on the street, and for them no driveway means no overnight charging. So the group least able to charge conveniently is the urban population, exactly the group cities most want to move out of petrol cars.

This graph shows how people in my city get to work. Cars were used by the most people in 2005, but they lost their top place about ten years later. Trains took over that top place and have stayed there since. Buses have simply gone down, year after year, and they have never come back up. The most surprising line is bicycles. They were almost flat until 2015, and after that they have shot up faster than anything else, though they are still not in first place.

話者1: Pine House sleeps up to sixty, our cooks make three meals a day, and the station for us is on the same line as your school, so no changing trains. We have had school groups here every summer for twenty years.
話者2: Hilltop Centre is on a direct line from the city and our kitchen staff serve breakfast, lunch and dinner. Do check the size, though. We have beds for twenty-eight guests only, so a group of forty could not all stay here.

Good morning. Most of you sorted your rubbish this week and felt you had done something useful. Today I want to look at what actually happens to it, and I should warn you that the picture is not flattering.

Begin with the numbers for plastic. Globally, about nine per cent of all plastic ever produced has been recycled. Twelve per cent has been burned. The remaining seventy-nine per cent is in landfill or in the environment. Note that this is a figure for the whole history of plastic, not for one bad year.

Why so low, when collection rates in many countries are high? The problem is that collection and recycling are different things. A household may sort perfectly, and the material may still be turned away further down the line. Some is contaminated with food. Some is a mixture of layers that no process can separate. And some has simply been produced in a form nobody has built a market for.

This is where the design of the product decides everything. A clear drinks bottle made of a single material can be turned back into a bottle many times. A pouch made of plastic film bonded to a metal layer cannot be pulled apart economically by any known method, no matter how carefully it is sorted.

So the decisive moment for a package is not the moment you put it in a bin. It is the moment an engineer chose its materials, years earlier and hundreds of kilometres away. Which suggests where regulation should point. Several countries now charge producers a fee that rises with how hard their packaging is to process, and that fee, unlike a public campaign, changes what gets designed.

A: My parents will be away this weekend, so we can have the movie night at my place.

Before you come to the river on Saturday, learn the order. What you do first is fill your bottle, holding it well below the surface so that no air gets in. Back at the tent, the water goes from the bottle into a clear tube — never test it in the bottle itself. Once it is in the tube, dip the paper strip and match the colour you get against the chart. Only then write the figures in your notebook. And we are not putting any fish back this year; that project ended in March.

Good afternoon. Tonight, while you sleep, your brain will be busy sorting through everything that happened today. Let me explain what we now know about sleep and memory.

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as a kind of switching off. Textbooks described the sleeping brain as idle, simply waiting for morning. Students were told that if they wanted to remember something, the answer was more hours of study, and sleep was time taken away from that study.

The picture changed in the nineteen nineties, when researchers began recording brain activity through the night. They found that the patterns produced while an animal learned a maze during the day were played again during sleep, faster and in the same order. Nothing was switching off at all.

We now think of sleep as the stage where a memory becomes permanent. During the day, new information is held in a small structure near the centre of the brain. At night, the same information is copied out to the outer surface, where it can last for years. Wake someone repeatedly during the deepest stage of sleep, and the copying never finishes.

There is a second effect, and it is easier to demonstrate. Give two groups a list of word pairs. Let one group sleep for eight hours and keep the other awake for the same eight hours. Test them the next evening, when both are equally tired. The group that slept remembers about forty per cent more. So sleep is not a gap in learning. It is part of the process, and it cannot be replaced by extra hours at the desk.

Reo: Imani, I have to place the order this evening. Run the four suppliers past me one last time.

Hana: It's the same in the library, and in the crowded corridors it's somehow even worse. I've started writing with my sleeves pulled over my hands, which does nothing at all for my handwriting.

Good morning. Today's topic is the bicycle sharing system, and I want to use it to show you how a small design decision can decide whether a public service works.

The first generation appeared in Amsterdam in nineteen sixty-five. White bicycles were left unlocked around the city for anyone to use. The idea was beautiful and it collapsed within a month, because almost every bicycle was stolen or thrown into a canal. For thirty years afterwards, city governments treated the whole concept as impossible.

The second generation added coin locks, but it did not fix the deeper problem. Nobody knew who had taken a bicycle, so nobody was answerable for it. What changed everything in the two thousands was not the bicycle. It was the card reader. Once each trip is linked to a named account, the bicycle stops being anonymous, and losses fall to a level a city can live with.

That brings us to today's numbers. In the largest systems, each bicycle is now used between four and eight times a day. Compare that with a privately owned bicycle, which sits unused for more than twenty-three hours out of twenty-four. The same piece of metal serves many more people.

And yet these systems rarely pay for themselves. Riders' fees typically cover about fifty per cent of the running cost. The heaviest expense is not repair. It is trucks, moving bicycles back uphill and out of the centre every night, because riders take them downhill in the morning and leave them there. Some cities now pay riders a small credit for returning a bicycle to an empty station, which is cheaper than sending a truck.

A: The people upstairs play loud music every night until midnight.
B: Have you talked to them directly?
A: I did, twice. They were friendly but nothing changed.
B: I see. I'll send a notice to all residents about quiet hours after ten.
A: Could you talk to them directly instead? A general notice might not work.

Good morning. Today's story is about the simplest medical intervention ever discovered, and about how long it took to be accepted.

Vienna, eighteen forty-seven. A young doctor named Semmelweis worked in a hospital with two maternity wards. In the first ward, staffed by doctors, about one mother in ten died after giving birth. In the second, staffed by midwives, the figure was closer to one in thirty. The wards took women on alternate days, so the patients were not different. Something about the first ward was killing them.

Semmelweis noticed that the doctors, unlike the midwives, came straight from performing autopsies. He could not explain why that mattered, because nobody yet knew that microbes existed. But he insisted that every doctor rinse his hands in a chlorine solution before entering the ward. Deaths in the first ward fell to the level of the second within a year.

And here is the uncomfortable part. His colleagues rejected him. Some were insulted by the suggestion that a gentleman's hands could be dirty. Others pointed out, correctly, that he had no theory to explain the result. Semmelweis was eventually dismissed from the hospital, and hand washing was not general practice for another forty years, until Pasteur's work made the mechanism clear.

The modern lesson is not just historical. Studies in today's hospitals find that staff clean their hands on well under half the occasions when guidelines require it. Good afternoon. Today's subject is attention, and I want to start by narrowing the question. The popular claim is that phones have shortened our attention spans permanently. That claim is much weaker than the evidence for something more specific and more interesting.

Begin with the well-established part. Switching between two tasks carries a cost. When you move from writing an essay to reading a message and back again, you do not resume where you left off. Part of your mind stays on the message, and studies put the recovery time at up to twenty minutes for demanding work. Over a day of frequent switching, that adds up to hours of reduced capacity.

Now the finding that surprised researchers. In one series of experiments, students sat a test with their phone either in another room, in a bag, or face down on the desk. The phone was silent in all three conditions. Scores were highest with the phone in another room and lowest with it on the desk, even though nobody in that group reported feeling distracted. The device did not have to do anything. Its presence was enough, because part of the mind was occupied with not looking at it.

So the important claim is not about damage. It is about location. And notice the practical consequence: turning off notifications is a smaller intervention than most people assume, because the effect measured here was produced by a silent phone.

One caution before we finish. These effects are averages, and the size varies a great deal between individuals. And permanent change in the brain is not what has been shown. Move the phone to another room and the capacity comes back the same afternoon.

Good morning. About one bite in three of the food on your plate exists because an insect visited a flower. Today I want to look at who those insects actually are.

When people talk about pollination, they usually mean one species: the honeybee. Honeybees are easy to keep, easy to move, and a single hive holds tens of thousands of workers. So for decades, growers of almonds, apples and blueberries have solved pollination by renting hives, trucking them in when the flowers open and taking them away afterwards.

That approach has been under pressure since two thousand six, when beekeepers in North America began losing around a third of their hives each winter. The causes are still argued about, but the effect on growers is simple. The price of renting a hive has roughly tripled in twenty years.

Here is the part that surprises people. Honeybees are not always the best pollinators. A honeybee packs pollen tightly onto its legs to carry it home, which means less of it rubs off on the next flower. A bumblebee is messier, and messier is better. Bumblebees also work in cool, wet weather that keeps honeybees inside the hive.

And wild insects are already doing far more than growers assume. Careful counts in orchards show that wild bees and flies, arriving with no rent to pay, carry out roughly half the pollination even in fields where hives have been placed. Those insects need hedges and rough ground near the orchard. A farm that removes every hedge to gain a little planting area is quietly paying for something it used to get free.

Good afternoon. Tonight, while you sleep, your brain will be busy sorting through everything that happened today. Let me explain what we now know about sleep and memory.

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as a kind of switching off. Textbooks described the sleeping brain as idle, simply waiting for morning. Students were told that if they wanted to remember something, the answer was more hours of study, and sleep was time taken away from that study.

The picture changed in the nineteen nineties, when researchers began recording brain activity through the night. They found that the patterns produced while an animal learned a maze during the day were played again during sleep, faster and in the same order. Nothing was switching off at all.

We now think of sleep as the stage where a memory becomes permanent. During the day, new information is held in a small structure near the centre of the brain. At night, the same information is copied out to the outer surface, where it can last for years. Wake someone repeatedly during the deepest stage of sleep, and the copying never finishes.

There is a second effect, and it is easier to demonstrate. Give two groups a list of word pairs. Let one group sleep for eight hours and keep the other awake for the same eight hours. Test them the next evening, when both are equally tired. The group that slept remembers about forty per cent more. So sleep is not a gap in learning. It is part of the process, and it cannot be replaced by extra hours at the desk.

Good morning. There are about seven thousand languages spoken today, and by the end of this century linguists expect roughly half of them to have no speakers left. I want to look at how that happens, and at what the standard response gets wrong.

First, how a language ends. It is almost never sudden. The usual pattern takes three generations. Grandparents speak the local language at home. Parents understand it but answer their own children in the national language, because that is the language of school and work. The grandchildren can follow a conversation but cannot produce a sentence. Nothing is banned and nobody decides. Each family simply makes a reasonable choice, and the sum of those choices ends a language.

Second, what linguists do about it. For most of the twentieth century, the response was documentation. Send a researcher, record the last fluent speakers, write a grammar and a dictionary, and place them in a university archive. The tapes are safe. Nobody listens to them.

And this is where I want to be blunt. A recorded language is not a living one. A grammar in an archive lets a scholar study a language; it does not let a child grow up in it. If the goal is speakers rather than data, the work has to happen where families make daily decisions.

There is one encouraging case. Hebrew had no native speakers for centuries and now has millions. But look at what it required: a state, a school system, and an army all operating in the language. No archive did that. Which means archives are worth keeping, but nobody should mistake them for a rescue.

Good morning. Today's story is about the simplest medical intervention ever discovered, and about how long it took to be accepted.

Vienna, eighteen forty-seven. A young doctor named Semmelweis worked in a hospital with two maternity wards. In the first ward, staffed by doctors, about one mother in ten died after giving birth. In the second, staffed by midwives, the figure was closer to one in thirty. The wards took women on alternate days, so the patients were not different. Something about the first ward was killing them.

Semmelweis noticed that the doctors, unlike the midwives, came straight from performing autopsies. He could not explain why that mattered, because nobody yet knew that microbes existed. But he insisted that every doctor rinse his hands in a chlorine solution before entering the ward. Deaths in the first ward fell to the level of the second within a year.

And here is the uncomfortable part. His colleagues rejected him. Some were insulted by the suggestion that a gentleman's hands could be dirty. Others pointed out, correctly, that he had no theory to explain the result. Semmelweis was eventually dismissed from the hospital, and hand washing was not general practice for another forty years, until Pasteur's work made the mechanism clear.

The modern lesson is not just historical. Studies in today's hospitals find that staff clean their hands on well under half the occasions when guidelines require it. And the reason given is almost never disagreement. It is time. A nurse on a busy ward may have dozens of such occasions in an hour, and the sink is not always close by. Good afternoon. Today's subject is attention, and I want to start by narrowing the question. The popular claim is that phones have shortened our attention spans permanently. That claim is much weaker than the evidence for something more specific and more interesting.

Begin with the well-established part. Switching between two tasks carries a cost. When you move from writing an essay to reading a message and back again, you do not resume where you left off. Part of your mind stays on the message, and studies put the recovery time at up to twenty minutes for demanding work. Over a day of frequent switching, that adds up to hours of reduced capacity.

Now the finding that surprised researchers. In one series of experiments, students sat a test with their phone either in another room, in a bag, or face down on the desk. The phone was silent in all three conditions. Scores were highest with the phone in another room and lowest with it on the desk, even though nobody in that group reported feeling distracted. The device did not have to do anything. Its presence was enough, because part of the mind was occupied with not looking at it.

So the important claim is not about damage. It is about location. And notice the practical consequence: turning off notifications is a smaller intervention than most people assume, because the effect measured here was produced by a silent phone.

One caution before we finish. These effects are averages, and the size varies a great deal between individuals. And permanent change in the brain is not what has been shown. Move the phone to another room and the capacity comes back the same afternoon.

Good morning. Today's topic is the bicycle sharing system, and I want to use it to show you how a small design decision can decide whether a public service works.

The first generation appeared in Amsterdam in nineteen sixty-five. White bicycles were left unlocked around the city for anyone to use. The idea was beautiful and it collapsed within a month, because almost every bicycle was stolen or thrown into a canal. For thirty years afterwards, city governments treated the whole concept as impossible.

The second generation added coin locks, but it did not fix the deeper problem. Nobody knew who had taken a bicycle, so nobody was answerable for it. What changed everything in the two thousands was not the bicycle. It was the card reader. Once each trip is linked to a named account, the bicycle stops being anonymous, and losses fall to a level a city can live with.

That brings us to today's numbers. In the largest systems, each bicycle is now used between four and eight times a day. Compare that with a privately owned bicycle, which sits unused for more than twenty-three hours out of twenty-four. The same piece of metal serves many more people.

Good morning. Electric cars are often discussed as a battery problem. I want to argue that the harder problem is where the electricity is delivered.

Start with the battery. In two thousand ten, a battery pack cost around one thousand one hundred dollars per kilowatt hour. Today it is under a hundred and forty. That is one of the fastest cost reductions in industrial history, and an electric car and a petrol car now cost roughly the same to build.

So why has adoption been so patchy? Survey after survey gives the same answer, and it is not price. Buyers say they are afraid of running out of charge on a long journey. Notice, though, that this fear does not match how people actually drive. The average daily distance in most countries is under fifty kilometres, well within any modern car's range. What buyers are really telling us is that they do not trust the network of charging points, not that they need a bigger battery.

And the numbers support them. Where those chargers sit is another matter. In several European countries there is one charger for every ten electric cars; in others the figure is one for every forty. Worse, roughly one in five public chargers is out of order at any moment, and a driver cannot know before arriving.

Which points to the real lesson. Home charging solves this for anyone with a driveway, and about eighty per cent of charging already happens overnight at home. But in cities, most people park on the street, and for them no driveway means no overnight charging. So the group least able to charge conveniently is the urban population, exactly the group cities most want to move out of petrol cars.

Good afternoon. Twenty years ago, a common prediction was that public libraries would close. The internet had arrived, everything was going online, and a building full of paper looked like a museum. That prediction turned out to be wrong, and the reason it was wrong is instructive.

Let me describe the old model first. A library was defined by what it held. Success was measured by the number of volumes on the shelves and the number of items borrowed each year. Staff spent much of their day at a desk, stamping cards and answering questions about where a book was located. The visitor's purpose was assumed: you came in, you took something away, you left.

Both of those measures did fall. In most countries, book lending peaked in the late nineteen nineties and has declined every year since. If holdings and loans were the only test, the prediction would have been right.

But visits did not fall with them. In many cities, the number of people walking through the door has risen, and what those people are doing inside has changed completely. They are using free internet access, sitting in a warm room, taking a language class, printing a job application, or letting a child attend a reading hour. In one large system, two thirds of visitors last year borrowed nothing at all.

So the library has quietly become something else: not a store of books, but a place a city provides where you are not required to buy anything. That is harder to count than loans, which is precisely the problem. When budgets are cut, the number that gets shown to politicians is still the number of loans, and by that number every library looks like it is failing.

Good afternoon. Tonight, while you sleep, your brain will be busy sorting through everything that happened today. Let me explain what we now know about sleep and memory.

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as a kind of switching off. Textbooks described the sleeping brain as idle, simply waiting for morning. Students were told that if they wanted to remember something, the answer was more hours of study, and sleep was time taken away from that study.

The picture changed in the nineteen nineties, when researchers began recording brain activity through the night. They found that the patterns produced while an animal learned a maze during the day were played again during sleep, faster and in the same order. Nothing was switching off at all.

We now think of sleep as the stage where a memory becomes permanent. During the day, new information is held in a small structure near the centre of the brain. At night, the same information is copied out to the outer surface, where it can last for years. Wake someone repeatedly during the deepest stage of sleep, and the copying never finishes.

There is a second effect, and it is easier to demonstrate. Give two groups a list of word pairs. Let one group sleep for eight hours and keep the other awake for the same eight hours. Test them the next evening, when both are equally tired. The group that slept remembers about forty per cent more. So sleep is not a gap in learning. It is part of the process, and it cannot be replaced by extra hours at the desk.

Good morning. On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be seven degrees warmer than the farmland outside it. That gap has a name, the urban heat island, and today I want to explain both why it exists and why the obvious remedy is more complicated than it looks.

The cause is mostly material. Asphalt and dark roofing absorb sunlight all day and give it back little by little all through the night, so a city never fully cools down before the next morning. Add the heat thrown out by air conditioners and engines, and you have a surface that stays warm around the clock.

Now, trees. A mature street tree does two things at once. Its canopy blocks sunlight before it reaches the pavement, and it releases water vapour from its leaves, which draws heat out of the air just as sweating does. Measurements under a good canopy show temperatures several degrees below the open street a few metres away.

But here is the difficulty. Cooling depends on canopy area, and canopy area takes decades. A tree planted this spring will provide almost no shade for fifteen years, and roughly a third of newly planted street trees die within five, usually from lack of water in their first two summers. So a planting programme announced today is a promise about the twenty-forties.

And the trees are not distributed evenly. In city after city, wealthy districts have two to three times the canopy of poor ones. The neighbourhoods with the least shade also tend to have the smallest homes and the fewest air conditioners. So the heat falls hardest on the people least equipped to escape it.

Hello everyone. When you picture plastic in the ocean, you probably picture a beach. Today I want to move your attention upstream, to rivers.

For twenty years, ocean clean-up campaigns focused almost entirely on the shoreline. Volunteers walked beaches with bags, and the photographs were powerful. But once plastic reaches open water, it breaks into pieces smaller than a grain of rice, and at that size no net can pick it up. Removing it out there costs roughly a hundred times what it costs to stop it on land.

That is why attention has shifted to rivers. A recent survey traced the plastic entering the sea and found something unexpected: a very small number of rivers carry the great majority of it. Just over a thousand rivers, out of about a hundred thousand worldwide, account for eighty per cent of the plastic reaching the ocean. Almost all of these are short rivers running through dense cities where waste collection has not kept pace with population growth.

This changes what a solution looks like. Instead of one global campaign, you can place barriers at a small number of specific points, because a floating barrier across a river mouth catches material while it is still large enough to grab.

But I want to be careful here. Barriers treat the symptom. The plastic still has to be paid for by someone, and in many of these cities the real gap is that rubbish is never picked up in the first place. A barrier is also useless during floods, when it must be opened. So the honest summary is this: rivers give us a cheaper place to act, not a complete answer.

Good afternoon. Twenty years ago, a common prediction was that public libraries would close. The internet had arrived, everything was going online, and a building full of paper looked like a museum. That prediction turned out to be wrong, and the reason it was wrong is instructive.

Let me describe the old model first. A library was defined by what it held. Success was measured by the number of volumes on the shelves and the number of items borrowed each year. Staff spent much of their day at a desk, stamping cards and answering questions about where a book was located. The visitor's purpose was assumed: you came in, you took something away, you left.

Both of those measures did fall. In most countries, book lending peaked in the late nineteen nineties and has declined every year since. If holdings and loans were the only test, the prediction would have been right.

But visits did not fall with them. In many cities, the number of people walking through the door has risen, and what those people are doing inside has changed completely. They are using free internet access, sitting in a warm room, taking a language class, printing a job application, or letting a child attend a reading hour. In one large system, two thirds of visitors last year borrowed nothing at all.

So the library has quietly become something else: not a store of books, but a place a city provides where you are not required to buy anything. That is harder to count than loans, which is precisely the problem. When budgets are cut, the number that gets shown to politicians is still the number of loans, and by that number every library looks like it is failing.
